newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Bracing for the FOMC meeting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Bracing for the FOMC meeting.

text.p: U.S. debt markets will likely have a quiet day on Friday as players square positions ahead of the long-awaited meeting of the Federal Reserve's policy-setting body on March 25, analysts said.
"I think it's going to be a quiet day ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee meeting next week," said Marilyn Schaja, economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp.
U.S. money market players appear to believe the odds for a Fed tightening next week increased after recent remarks by the central bank Chairman Alan Greenspan.

"I think he (Greenspan) is telling you the Fed is ready to tighten. I don't think it's a done deal yet, but I think the odds are in favor of a rate hike next week. It shouldn't surprise anybody if the Fed does that," Schaja said.
Greenspan said on Thursday that the Fed must look ahead in its policy to avoid being "behind the curve."
The chairman, testifying before the Congress' Joint Economic Committee, also said the Fed needs to look beyond current data due to policy lag effect.
"Those are signals that the Fed might tighten in March," said a money trader at a U.S. investment bank.

A mixed performance of the U.S. Treasury market on Thursday, which saw short-end prices dropping and long-end prices rising, was also seen as an indication that players are pricing in a Fed tightening next week, traders said.
The spread between the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond and the two-year note narrowed sharply on Thursday to 71 basis points from 77 basis points on Wednesday and 80 basis points on March 13.
"The short-end of the curve has pretty much priced in a Fed move. It's just about priced in," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc.
"But that doesn't mean that we could trade a bit lower if the Fed does move," Iggo added.
The 30-year bond yield has shown some strong resistance around the 7.0 percent area. Once again on Thursday the yield tested that level and retraced on techinical buying.
Analysts said, however, that if the Fed does hike the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25, the long bond yield could break that barrier.
"I see the long-end a little bit above (the 7.0 percent level). But not significantly above ... maybe 7.10 or 7.15 percent," DLJ's Schaja said.
Analysts said the lack of fresh key economic data on Friday is also likely to keep the market quiet.
On Friday, the market will take in some second-tier data, including import and export prices and the federal budget. The two reports are for the month of February.
The benchmark bond ended Thursday session up 12/32 at 95-27/32 to yield 6.96 percent. The two-year note was down 2/32 at 99-10/32 to yield 6.25 percent.

The Fed added temporary reserves to the banking system on Thursday through overnight and a seven-day fixed system repurchase agreements. The two operations combined injected $7.839 billion into the system.
Federal funds are seen opening at 5.19 percent on Friday.
